source.title: Ladder Up, Memory Down: Low-Cost Fine-Tuning With Side Nets
source.authors: E. Zheng; Nathan Cerisara; Sébastien Warichet; Emmanuel Helbert; Christophe Cerisara

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling relationships in fine-tuning, a training-stage setting different from the pretraining laws in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper fits held-out test-loss scaling laws for fine-tuning and downstream error-versus-compute laws; these results are recorded below. It does not test pretraining loss scaling or out-of-fit extrapolation. Math benchmark and architecture-ablation accuracies are not rows for the loss-based versions; reported comparisons with cited prior work are not treated as this study's results.
record.test_reason: Fits power-law laws to its own fine-tuning runs: held-out test loss against dataset size (Table 1) and downstream error against compute (Table 8). This bears on V5 (fine-tuning regime), V6 (downstream predictability) and narrowly on V7 (NLS vs Huber fit). The backbone is frozen and data spans only 50k–400k samples, under one order of magnitude. The authors say they assume the law rather than validate it.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors claim Ladder matches QLoRA's compute-scaling slope (Finding 1) and offers comparable accuracy-per-compute with a 'more stable scaling slope' (Finding 2). Their Appendix D.5.2 says the scaling law is assumed, not validated, and needs broader sweeps and extrapolation tests. The paraphrase omits that downstream Ladder β estimates are systematically lower than QLoRA's; the authors describe them as similar within uncertainty.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tuning rather than pretraining; fixed pretrained backbones with Ladder or QLoRA adapters; test loss is fitted against dataset size and converted to compute, while downstream error-compute laws are also fitted. No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation law is derived.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports results under nonlinear least squares and Huber loss fitting; fitted λ slopes are described as similar. Downstream exponent estimates vary by model family and method, with broad intervals.

fits_no_version.finding: Adapter (Ladder side network) width 160–224 shows no clear consistent effect on CoLA/MRPC scores. The optimal adapter depth and connection position are task-dependent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Side-adapter shape affects fine-tuned accuracy only modestly. This is analogous to V4, but for adapters and accuracy rather than backbone shape and loss.

record.problems: Scaling-law robustness is tested on few model families. Downstream compute sampling is sparse and bootstrap intervals are broad. The authors state they do not fully validate the assumed scaling law or test out-of-fit extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results omitted. Architecture and math benchmark accuracy results were excluded because the listed loss-based versions are not measured by those results.

untested.parts: All of it. No pretraining loss is measured, and parameters and tokens are not varied over orders of magnitude.
All of it. The authors state no out-of-fit extrapolation test was done.
All of it. There is no allocation trend across budgets; the single xLadder isoFLOP curve (Fig. 19) is memory-limited to its left side.
All of it. The backbone shape is not varied; the adapter width and depth ablations report accuracy only.
Other modalities, repeated data, and transfer. Whether the power-law form holds beyond about one decade of fine-tuning data, or for backbone-size scaling.
Prediction from pretraining loss, extrapolation to unseen scales, and tasks beyond CoLA/QQP.
Parameter counting, training schedule, data choice, compute-optimal splits, and curvature away from a power law.

missing.what: xLadder isoFLOP test-loss curve on a Qwen2.5-14B backbone, varying side-network size at fixed compute. The curve reaches only its left side before running out of memory.
missing.versions: V3 (context only; not an allocation trend)

record.verdict_notes: Compute in the loss law is C = ζ·Df, so compute variation is only data variation over 50k–400k samples with a frozen backbone. The 'power law' rests on 5 points spanning under one decade, with no goodness-of-fit reported. The V7 challenge is weak: it concerns only NLS vs Huber on the same data. The abstract's claim that Ladder matches QLoRA's slope applies to test loss (λ); downstream β point estimates for Ladder are roughly half QLoRA's.

versions.untested_parts: The measured loss is from fine-tuning, not held-out pretraining loss; the study does not vary parameter count, tokens, and compute under the claim's non-bottleneck conditions.
No out-of-fit extrapolation test is reported; the paper explicitly says it cannot fully validate extrapolation.
No sweep across compute budgets establishes how compute-optimal parameter and token counts grow. The single practical isoFLOP discussion does not establish a stable allocation trend.
The architecture comparisons report downstream accuracy, not loss.
Tests fine-tuning, including side tuning, but not other modalities, repeated data, transfer, or fine-tuning regimes beyond the reported setups.
Tests downstream error versus compute in the reported fine-tuning tasks and model families; does not test prediction from pretraining loss or extrapolation to untested scales and tasks.
Compares two fitting procedures for the fine-tuning test-loss law. Does not test parameter-counting choices, compute-optimal splits across budgets, or whether curves bend away from a power law.
